html:
An observatory founded in 1259 at Maragheh in northwestern Iran by the astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, paid for by Hulagu Khan, the Mongol founder of the Ilkhanate. Hulagu had sacked Baghdad the year before.

It was one of the first observatories run as a full research institution, with large instruments, a big library and a staff of astronomers from across the Islamic world and even one from China. After about twelve years of observation it produced the Ilkhanic Tables of 1272, used to compute the positions of the planets.

Al-Tusi and his colleagues searched for better models of the planets than those of Ptolemy. Al-Tusi's device, the Tusi couple, turns two circular motions into a straight line. Similar ideas appear later in the work of Nicolaus Copernicus, and historians still debate whether he learned of them. The observatory declined in the 14th century, but it inspired Ulugh Beg's observatory in Samarkand and others.
